OAI coordinates four main training tracks for district staff:

Each track has its own coordinator, budget line, and evaluation plan. The UDL Cohort is the only track that requires a multi-month commitment from participants. The others are structured as ongoing meetings or single-day events.

---

**3. Annual Training Cycle (September 2024 – June 2026)**

All OAI training follows a standard annual cycle, regardless of the specific track. The cycle is designed to align with the academic calendar and to allow schools to plan their professional development calendars in advance.

| **Cycle Phase** | **Timing** | **Activities** |
|-----------------|------------|----------------|
| Planning & Needs Assessment | March – May | Review of previous year's evaluation data; school surveys; budget allocation |
| Cohort Recruitment & Selection | June – August | Application window; principal nominations; cohort roster finalization |
| Program Delivery | September – April | Monthly sessions (UDL Cohort); bi-monthly Liaison Network meetings; ATLL sessions as scheduled |
| Evaluation & Reporting | May – June | Post-surveys, classroom observation data, outcome reports to the District Board |
| Revision & Re-Approval | June – July | Program revisions based on evaluation; re-approval of programs for the next school year |

This cycle is the same for all four tracks. The UDL Cohort follows this cycle strictly, with the exception that its recruitment window opens two weeks earlier than the other tracks to accommodate the application review process.

---

**4. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Cohort – Program Description**

Office of Accessibility and Inclusion adopted_training_program Universal Design for Learning Cohort. Record status: current.

The UDL Cohort is a professional learning community focused on the practical application of Universal Design for Learning principles in K–12 classrooms. The program runs from September through April, with eight full-day sessions and two half-day follow-up sessions in May.

**4.1 Program Goals**

- Increase teacher confidence in designing lessons that address learner variability.
- Reduce the number of accommodation requests by embedding flexibility into core instruction.
- Build a network of UDL-trained teachers who can serve as building-level resources after the cohort ends.
- Align classroom practices with the district's inclusive education policy (Board Policy 4260).

**4.2 Participant Profile**

- Classroom teachers (grades K–12), special education teachers, instructional coaches, and intervention specialists.
- Participants are selected through a joint application and principal nomination process.
- Each school may nominate up to three staff members per year. Exceptions are made for schools with high rates of accommodation requests or those in their first year of a school improvement plan.

**4.3 Session Structure**

Sessions are held monthly at the district's Central Services Building, Room 214. Each session includes:

- A content block (90 minutes) covering a specific UDL principle or practice.
- A collaborative planning block (60 minutes) where participants work on their own lesson materials.
- A reflection and feedback block (30 minutes) with structured peer observation protocols.

Between sessions, participants are expected to implement at least one UDL-aligned strategy in their classroom and bring student work samples to the next session.
3.  **Session Attendance and Make-Up Policy.** Participants may miss no more than one full-day session and one half-day session to receive full completion credit. Make-up work for missed sessions will consist of a recorded session review and a written reflection aligned to the session's learning objectives. This policy is unchanged from the pilot, but it is now formally codified.

4.  **Stipend and Sub Release.** Participants will continue to receive a $500 stipend upon successful completion of the program. Sub release funding is available for all eight full-day sessions and the two half-day follow-ups. Schools are asked to schedule sub releases in the OAI portal at least two weeks in advance.

5.  **Building-Level Resource Designation.** Teachers who complete the cohort will be designated as building-level UDL resources for two years following completion. This designation includes a light-touch expectation to serve on their school's instructional leadership team or equivalent. This designation is now an official role recognized in the district's staffing guidelines.

**Section 4: Related Training Initiatives and Professional Development Offerings**

The UDL Cohort operates within a broader framework of accessibility-focused professional development offered by the Office of Accessibility and Inclusion. The following initiatives complement the cohort and are available to district staff. Participation in one initiative does not preclude enrollment in another, though scheduling conflicts should be reviewed with site administrators.

**4.1 Accessibility Liaison Network (ALN)**

The Accessibility Liaison Network is a year-round, site-based role designed to create a direct line of communication between each school and the Office of Accessibility and Inclusion. Each school site selects one staff member to serve as its Accessibility Liaison. Liaisons are not released from their primary teaching or support duties; the role is an additional responsibility with a small stipend paid quarterly.

Liaison responsibilities include:

- Attending monthly virtual meetings (second Tuesday, 3:30–4:30 PM)
- Disseminating accessibility-related announcements to site staff
- Collecting and forwarding site-level accessibility concerns to the district office
- Assisting with the coordination of accommodation requests during state testing windows
- Maintaining a physical bulletin board or digital equivalent with current accessibility resources

The network was established in Fall 2023 and has operated continuously since. The 2025–2026 liaison roster includes representatives from all 14 district sites. Meeting attendance is tracked, and liaisons who miss three consecutive meetings without prior notice are contacted by the office to confirm continued participation. This is a standing expectation for the role.

The ALN does not provide formal training; its purpose is coordination and communication. Staff seeking skill-building opportunities should reference the Professional Development Module series described in Section 4.2 or the UDL Cohort described in Section 2.

**4.2 Professional Development Module Series**

The Office of Accessibility and Inclusion maintains a catalog of self-paced online modules. These modules are hosted on the district's professional development portal and are available to all certificated and classified staff. Modules are designed to be completed independently, and each takes approximately 45–60 minutes to finish.

**Program Evaluation Summary – Q1 2026**
**Accessibility Training Program**
**Prepared by:** Sarah Okafor, Program Evaluator
**Date:** April 14, 2026
**Distribution:** Office of Accessibility and Inclusion; Building Administrators; Professional Development Committee

---

**1. Overview**

This summary covers the period January 1 – March 31, 2026, and focuses on the implementation of the five core training modules (ACC-101 through ACC-105), the two specialty modules (ACC-106 and ACC-107), and the IEP/504 module (ACC-108). The evaluation draws on completion data from the learning management system, attendance records from facilitated sessions, and interviews with eleven building administrators and fourteen staff members across six schools. Overall, the program continues to show steady growth in both volume and reach, but several structural issues remain that will require attention in Q2.

**2. Strengths Observed**

The most notable strength this quarter is the continued high volume in ACC-101 and ACC-108. These modules remain the entry points for most staff, and the February new-hire cohort (n=47) accounted for a substantial portion of completions. This suggests that the onboarding process is effectively routing new staff to the appropriate foundational training.

School-level adoption also improved. Lincoln High School's full-staff push in February was well-organized and resulted in a measurable increase in active certificated staff. Maplewood Middle School's PLC study group for ACC-108 is a model worth replicating; the 12 staff who completed the module together reported higher confidence in applying IEP accommodations in daily practice. The lunch-and-learn format at Cedar Ridge Elementary for ACC-103 was also well-received, with 71% of certificated staff active.

The sensory-friendly classroom module (ACC-107) continues to have the lowest completion volume, but this is expected given its targeted audience. Interviews with special education teachers who did complete it indicate high satisfaction and practical utility. We are not concerned about low volume at this time; the module is not flagged as underperforming.

**3. Areas for Improvement**

**3.1. Accessible Document Creation (ACC-103)**
While Cedar Ridge Elementary hosted a successful lunch-and-learn, overall completion for ACC-103 remains below the district average. The module is often described by staff as "useful but dry," and several teachers noted that the examples used in the online version are oriented toward office documents rather than classroom materials. This is a minor content issue, but it may be dampening engagement. I recommend the Office of Accessibility and Inclusion review the module examples and consider adding a classroom-specific scenario.

**3.2. Communication and Autism Spectrum Supports (ACC-106)**
Completion rates for ACC-106 are adequate, but interviews with paraprofessionals revealed a recurring concern: the module does not address non-speaking students who use augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices. This was raised independently by staff at three different schools. The module is not inaccurate, but the omission is increasingly noticeable as more students use AAC in general education settings. I recommend a content update in Q3, with input from the district's speech-language pathologists.

**3.3. Universal Design for Learning (ACC-105)**
ACC-105 has the second-highest completion volume, but the evaluation found that many completions are "click-through" rather than genuine engagement. The average time spent in the module is 22 minutes, which is significantly below the estimated 45-minute completion time. This suggests that staff are completing the module quickly without fully absorbing the content. I recommend adding a short knowledge check at the midpoint of the module to encourage active engagement. This is a process issue, not a content issue.
**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** District Principals, Assistant Principals, and School Accessibility Coordinators
**FROM:** Office of Accessibility and Inclusion
**DATE:** November 16, 2026
**RE:** Upcoming Training Initiatives and Schedule for Spring 2027

This memo outlines the planned accessibility training activities for the remainder of the 2026-27 school year. Please review the tentative schedule below and share relevant items with your staff. We welcome feedback through your building's accessibility coordinator or by contacting our office directly.

---

**1. Annual Compliance Training Refresh (ACC-100)**

The annual compliance training refresh will be offered again in January. As in prior years, completion is required for all certificated and classified staff. The course will remain the same format as the 2026 version; we are not planning substantive content changes at this time. The training window will open on **January 11, 2027**, and close on **February 26, 2027**.

We will send a separate communication with login instructions and the list of staff who must complete the training. Please note that new hires who joined after the fall window will be included in this cohort.

---

**2. Module Updates and Revisions**

Based on the annual evaluation and feedback collected this fall, the following updates are scheduled. These timelines are tentative and depend on the availability of our content review committee.

**2.1. Accessible Document Creation (ACC-103)**
As noted in the evaluation summary, this module has been described as "useful but dry." We have begun working with two classroom teachers from Cedar Ridge and Lincoln Middle to develop a classroom-specific scenario. The revised module is expected to be available by **February 15, 2027**. We will not require staff who completed the current version to retake the entire module; only the new scenario will be added as an optional supplement.

**2.2. Communication and Autism Spectrum Supports (ACC-106)**
We are convening a small workgroup of speech-language pathologists to review the module for updates regarding augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices. The workgroup will meet in early December. Our goal is to have a revised version ready for the spring professional development catalog, with a target release of **March 1, 2027**. We anticipate the update will add a new section on supporting non-speaking students in general education settings, but the scope has not been finalized.

**2.3. Universal Design for Learning (ACC-105)**
To address the "click-through" completions identified in the evaluation, we are adding a short knowledge check at the midpoint of the module. This is a simple process change and does not alter the content. The updated module is scheduled for release on **January 25, 2027**. We will also adjust the estimated completion time in the catalog to reflect the added check.

---

**3. New Training Modules in Development**

The following modules are in the early stages of development. Details are subject to change as we work with our advisory committee.

**3.1. Supporting Students with Diabetes and Other Health Conditions (ACC-201)**
This module is being developed in partnership with the district nursing staff. It will cover basic responsibilities for classroom staff, including recognizing symptoms of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, understanding emergency care plans, and communicating with the school nurse. We expect the module to be available for the fall 2027 semester. The content outline is currently being drafted.

OAI coordinates four main training tracks for district staff:

Each track has its own coordinator, budget line, and evaluation plan. The UDL Cohort is the only track that requires a multi-month commitment from participants. The others are structured as ongoing meetings or single-day events.

---

**3. Annual Training Cycle (September 2024 – June 2026)**

All OAI training follows a standard annual cycle, regardless of the specific track. The cycle is designed to align with the academic calendar and to allow schools to plan their professional development calendars in advance.

| **Cycle Phase** | **Timing** | **Activities** |
|-----------------|------------|----------------|
| Planning & Needs Assessment | March – May | Review of previous year's evaluation data; school surveys; budget allocation |
| Cohort Recruitment & Selection | June – August | Application window; principal nominations; cohort roster finalization |
| Program Delivery | September – April | Monthly sessions (UDL Cohort); bi-monthly Liaison Network meetings; ATLL sessions as scheduled |
| Evaluation & Reporting | May – June | Post-surveys, classroom observation data, outcome reports to the District Board |
| Revision & Re-Approval | June – July | Program revisions based on evaluation; re-approval of programs for the next school year |

This cycle is the same for all four tracks. The UDL Cohort follows this cycle strictly, with the exception that its recruitment window opens two weeks earlier than the other tracks to accommodate the application review process.

---

**4. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Cohort – Program Description**

Office of Accessibility and Inclusion adopted_training_program Universal Design for Learning Cohort. Record status: current.

The UDL Cohort is a professional learning community focused on the practical application of Universal Design for Learning principles in K–12 classrooms. The program runs from September through April, with eight full-day sessions and two half-day follow-up sessions in May.

**4.1 Program Goals**

- Increase teacher confidence in designing lessons that address learner variability.
- Reduce the number of accommodation requests by embedding flexibility into core instruction.
- Build a network of UDL-trained teachers who can serve as building-level resources after the cohort ends.
- Align classroom practices with the district's inclusive education policy (Board Policy 4260).

**4.2 Participant Profile**

- Classroom teachers (grades K–12), special education teachers, instructional coaches, and intervention specialists.
- Participants are selected through a joint application and principal nomination process.
- Each school may nominate up to three staff members per year. Exceptions are made for schools with high rates of accommodation requests or those in their first year of a school improvement plan.

**4.3 Session Structure**

Sessions are held monthly at the district's Central Services Building, Room 214. Each session includes:

- A content block (90 minutes) covering a specific UDL principle or practice.
- A collaborative planning block (60 minutes) where participants work on their own lesson materials.
- A reflection and feedback block (30 minutes) with structured peer observation protocols.

Between sessions, participants are expected to implement at least one UDL-aligned strategy in their classroom and bring student work samples to the next session.

**Accessibility Training Program Documentation**

**Section 4: Related Training Initiatives and Professional Development Offerings**

The UDL Cohort operates within a broader framework of accessibility-focused professional development offered by the Office of Accessibility and Inclusion. The following initiatives complement the cohort and are available to district staff. Participation in one initiative does not preclude enrollment in another, though scheduling conflicts should be reviewed with site administrators.

**4.1 Accessibility Liaison Network (ALN)**

The Accessibility Liaison Network is a year-round, site-based role designed to create a direct line of communication between each school and the Office of Accessibility and Inclusion. Each school site selects one staff member to serve as its Accessibility Liaison. Liaisons are not released from their primary teaching or support duties; the role is an additional responsibility with a small stipend paid quarterly.

Liaison responsibilities include:

- Attending monthly virtual meetings (second Tuesday, 3:30–4:30 PM)
- Disseminating accessibility-related announcements to site staff
- Collecting and forwarding site-level accessibility concerns to the district office
- Assisting with the coordination of accommodation requests during state testing windows
- Maintaining a physical bulletin board or digital equivalent with current accessibility resources

The network was established in Fall 2023 and has operated continuously since. The 2025–2026 liaison roster includes representatives from all 14 district sites. Meeting attendance is tracked, and liaisons who miss three consecutive meetings without prior notice are contacted by the office to confirm continued participation. This is a standing expectation for the role.

The ALN does not provide formal training; its purpose is coordination and communication. Staff seeking skill-building opportunities should reference the Professional Development Module series described in Section 4.2 or the UDL Cohort described in Section 2.

**4.2 Professional Development Module Series**

The Office of Accessibility and Inclusion maintains a catalog of self-paced online modules. These modules are hosted on the district's professional development portal and are available to all certificated and classified staff. **Program Evaluation Summary – Q1 2026**
**Accessibility Training Program**
**Prepared by:** Sarah Okafor, Program Evaluator
**Date:** April 14, 2026
**Distribution:** Office of Accessibility and Inclusion; Building Administrators; Professional Development Committee

---

**1. Overview**

This summary covers the period January 1 – March 31, 2026, and focuses on the implementation of the five core training modules (ACC-101 through ACC-105), the two specialty modules (ACC-106 and ACC-107), and the IEP/504 module (ACC-108). The evaluation draws on completion data from the learning management system, attendance records from facilitated sessions, and interviews with eleven building administrators and fourteen staff members across six schools. Overall, the program continues to show steady growth in both volume and reach, but several structural issues remain that will require attention in Q2.

**2. Strengths Observed**

The most notable strength this quarter is the continued high volume in ACC-101 and ACC-108. These modules remain the entry points for most staff, and the February new-hire cohort (n=47) accounted for a substantial portion of completions. This suggests that the onboarding process is effectively routing new staff to the appropriate foundational training.

School-level adoption also improved. Lincoln High School's full-staff push in February was well-organized and resulted in a measurable increase in active certificated staff. Maplewood Middle School's PLC study group for ACC-108 is a model worth replicating; the 12 staff who completed the module together reported higher confidence in applying IEP accommodations in daily practice. The lunch-and-learn format at Cedar Ridge Elementary for ACC-103 was also well-received, with 71% of certificated staff active.

The sensory-friendly classroom module (ACC-107) continues to have the lowest completion volume, but this is expected given its targeted audience. Interviews with special education teachers who did complete it indicate high satisfaction and practical utility. We are not concerned about low volume at this time; the module is not flagged as underperforming.

**3. Areas for Improvement**

**3.1. Accessible Document Creation (ACC-103)**
While Cedar Ridge Elementary hosted a successful lunch-and-learn, overall completion for ACC-103 remains below the district average. The module is often described by staff as "useful but dry," and several teachers noted that the examples used in the online version are oriented toward office documents rather than classroom materials. This is a minor content issue, but it may be dampening engagement. I recommend the Office of Accessibility and Inclusion review the module examples and consider adding a classroom-specific scenario.

**3.2. Communication and Autism Spectrum Supports (ACC-106)**
Completion rates for ACC-106 are adequate, but interviews with paraprofessionals revealed a recurring concern: the module does not address non-speaking students who use augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices. This was raised independently by staff at three different schools. The module is not inaccurate, but the omission is increasingly noticeable as more students use AAC in general education settings. I recommend a content update in Q3, with input from the district's speech-language pathologists.

**3.3. Universal Design for Learning (ACC-105)**
ACC-105 has the second-highest completion volume, but the evaluation found that many completions are "click-through" rather than genuine engagement. The average time spent in the module is 22 minutes, which is significantly below the estimated 45-minute completion time. This suggests that staff are completing the module quickly without fully absorbing the content. I recommend adding a short knowledge check at the midpoint of the module to encourage active engagement. This is a process issue, not a content issue.

**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** District Principals, Assistant Principals, and School Accessibility Coordinators
**FROM:** Office of Accessibility and Inclusion
**DATE:** November 16, 2026
**RE:** Upcoming Training Initiatives and Schedule for Spring 2027

This memo outlines the planned accessibility training activities for the remainder of the 2026-27 school year. Please review the tentative schedule below and share relevant items with your staff. We welcome feedback through your building's accessibility coordinator or by contacting our office directly.

---

**1. Annual Compliance Training Refresh (ACC-100)**

The annual compliance training refresh will be offered again in January. As in prior years, completion is required for all certificated and classified staff. The course will remain the same format as the 2026 version; we are not planning substantive content changes at this time. The training window will open on **January 11, 2027**, and close on **February 26, 2027**.

We will send a separate communication with login instructions and the list of staff who must complete the training. Please note that new hires who joined after the fall window will be included in this cohort.

---

**2. Module Updates and Revisions**

Based on the annual evaluation and feedback collected this fall, the following updates are scheduled. These timelines are tentative and depend on the availability of our content review committee.

**2.1. Accessible Document Creation (ACC-103)**
As noted in the evaluation summary, this module has been described as "useful but dry." We have begun working with two classroom teachers from Cedar Ridge and Lincoln Middle to develop a classroom-specific scenario. The revised module is expected to be available by **February 15, 2027**. We will not require staff who completed the current version to retake the entire module; only the new scenario will be added as an optional supplement.

**2.2. Communication and Autism Spectrum Supports (ACC-106)**
We are convening a small workgroup of speech-language pathologists to review the module for updates regarding augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices. The workgroup will meet in early December. Our goal is to have a revised version ready for the spring professional development catalog, with a target release of **March 1, 2027**. We anticipate the update will add a new section on supporting non-speaking students in general education settings, but the scope has not been finalized.

**2.3. Universal Design for Learning (ACC-105)**
To address the "click-through" completions identified in the evaluation, we are adding a short knowledge check at the midpoint of the module. This is a simple process change and does not alter the content. The updated module is scheduled for release on **January 25, 2027**. We will also adjust the estimated completion time in the catalog to reflect the added check.

---

**3. New Training Modules in Development**

The following modules are in the early stages of development. Details are subject to change as we work with our advisory committee.

**3.1. Supporting Students with Diabetes and Other Health Conditions (ACC-201)**
This module is being developed in partnership with the district nursing staff. It will cover basic responsibilities for classroom staff, including recognizing symptoms of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, understanding emergency care plans, and communicating with the school nurse. We expect the module to be available for the fall 2027 semester. The content outline is currently being drafted.
